docs.title: Fill-A-Bot Pump Control
docs.text: Clay Belsher | EGR 304

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text: Fill-A-Bot is an automated water-dispensing system that fills a container to a selected amount. The main controller coordinates the user controls, measurement subsystems, and pump board to start dispensing and stop at the target. My responsibility is the pump-control subsystem, including its local power circuit, motor driver, and digital command connections.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
My board uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to receive two digital command signals from the main controller. CMD0 connects to RC3, CMD1 connects to RC2, and ribbon pin 8 provides a common ground. RA2 controls the motor-switching circuit.

The board includes a barrel-jack power input, fuse, 5V linear regulator, motor flyback protection, and a debug LED and button. The current single-MOSFET driver requires an H-bridge revision for forward-and-reverse operation. The linked design pages explain the component choices, configuration, calculations, and remaining decisions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
My subsystem controls the Fill-A-Bot water pump. The main control board sends two digital command signals through the ribbon connector: CMD0 connects to RC3, and CMD1 connects to RC2. Ribbon pin 8 provides a common ground between boards.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano reads these inputs and controls the MOSFET through RA2. The MOSFET switches the pump’s connection to ground. The gate resistor limits current during switching, and the pull-down resistor keeps the MOSFET off when the control output is not driving it. The 1N5822 flyback diode provides a path for motor current when the MOSFET switches off, limiting the voltage spike.

The barrel jack supplies power locally. The L7805 provides a 5V supply for the control electronics, while the pump uses the motor supply directly. Power is not supplied through the ribbon connector.

docs.title: Design Decisions
docs.text:
The main controller sends a two-bit pump command, written as C1 C0. Ribbon pin 1 carries C1 to RC3, and ribbon pin 2 carries C0 to RC2. The commands are 00 = Stop, 01 = Run, 10 = Stop, and 11 = Stop. The pump runs only while the command is 01. Ribbon pin 8 provides common ground.

The motor uses a separate power path because it requires more current than a microcontroller pin can supply. All control and motor grounds share a common reference.

docs.title: Remaining Design Work
docs.text:
The current single-MOSFET circuit supports one-direction operation. An H-bridge is still needed to meet the forward-and-reverse requirement.

The diagram currently shows a 12V supply. This must be reconciled with the project’s specified 9V adapter before the power design is finalized. Motor current, regulator heating, and the Curiosity Nano external-power configuration also need verification.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text: Clay Belsher — Fill-A-Bot Pump Control Subsystem

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
My subsystem controls the pump that moves water from the reservoir to the container. The main controller sends two digital command signals to my board. My controller reads those signals and controls the motor circuit.

The main controller determines when the selected amount has been dispensed and sends the command to stop the pump. Filling accuracy depends on the complete system, including measurement, communication, pump response, and water remaining in the tubing.

Current design status: The schematic and original component comparisons use a 12V supply. The project specifies a 9V adapter, so the supply selection and pump performance at that voltage still need confirmation. The current single-MOSFET circuit supports one-direction operation. An H-bridge is needed to meet the forward-and-reverse requirement.

The tables below document the component comparisons and explain the current choices. Prices are earlier estimates in USD, excluding shipping and taxes. Prices, availability, and specifications need checking before ordering.

docs.title: Water Pump
docs.text:
The pump needs to move water at a useful rate, fit the tubing arrangement, and work with the final supply. The required reverse operation also needs checking with the actual pump mechanism. Reversing motor rotation does not automatically mean the pump will reverse water flow.

Startup and stall current need confirmation.Actual flow at the final supply voltage needs testing.Reverse-flow capability and dripping after stopping are not verified. Adafruit 1150 Peristaltic PumpProduct information $24.95 Water stays inside replaceable tubing.Lower flow may make small fills easier to control.Tubing can be removed for cleaning or replacement. Originally compared as a 12V option.Lower flow increases filling time.Tubing wear can change performance, and this option costs more. DFRobot FIT0200 Immersible PumpProduct information $9.20 Lower listed cost.Compact arrangement inside the reservoir.Advertised flow could suit larger fills. Must remain submerged during operation.Removal and cleaning are more involved.Suitability for small fills, the final voltage, and reverse operation needs confirmation.

Current selection: Gikfun EK1856 / R385, pending requirement checks.

Why I chose it: I originally chose the R385 because it fit the planned external tubing arrangement and offered a useful advertised flow rate at a lower cost than the peristaltic option. It also lets us mount the pump outside the reservoir.

What still needs checking: I do not have the pump yet. I need to confirm performance at the required supply voltage, operating and startup current, and whether this pump can perform the reverse operation the system needs. If it cannot, the pump selection must change.

Custom option considered: Building the pump itself would add work on sealing, moving parts, and consistent flow. A purchased pump lets us focus on the control board and dispensing performance.

docs.title: Motor Switching — Current MOSFET Circuit
docs.text:
The microcontroller controls the motor circuit but does not supply motor current directly. The current schematic uses a low-side MOSFET switch. A gate resistor limits gate-charging current, and a pull-down resistor holds the gate low when the controller is not driving it.

These comparisons apply to the current single-MOSFET circuit. They do not represent a completed H-bridge selection.

Option Estimated Unit Cost Pros Cons AOS AOTF2618LManufacturer information $1.90 Originally selected for the planned logic-level gate drive.Voltage rating provides margin above the nominal motor supply.Symbol and footprint are already included in the project. Availability needs checking.Needs gate components and motor-current protection.Current, switching loss, and temperature still need verification. Infineon IRLZ44NPBFDatasheet $1.80 Logic-level MOSFET option.Through-hole package is convenient for assembly and testing.Considered as an alternative to the current part. Pinout and footprint must be checked before substitution.Gate drive and switching frequency need review.The drain-connected metal tab affects mounting. Infineon IRLB8721PBFDatasheet $2.25 Low on-resistance can reduce conduction loss.Logic-level gate-drive option.Through-hole package is convenient for prototyping. Lower voltage rating than the other compared parts.Highest estimated price in this comparison.Gate drive, footprint, and temperature need verification.

Component in the current schematic: AOTF2618L.

Why I chose it: I originally chose the AOTF2618L for the planned 5V control signal and motor supply. Having its symbol and footprint in the project also made it convenient to include in the schematic. Its final suitability depends on the actual gate voltage, motor current, and temperature.

Supporting components: R1 is the 1kΩ series gate resistor. R2 is the 10kΩ gate pull-down resistor. JP1 provides an enable jumper in the control path. These components support the current switching circuit; they do not provide direction control.

Required revision: One low-side MOSFET cannot reverse the motor. I need to replace this switching arrangement with an H-bridge that supports the final supply voltage, startup and stall current, and controller logic levels. Motor-current recirculation protection must match that design.

Custom option considered: A discrete H-bridge or an integrated H-bridge IC could provide direction control. The final choice has not been made. The motor-control circuitry must be built on our board rather than supplied by a peripheral daughterboard.

docs.title: 5V Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
The control electronics use a planned 5V rail. The assignment requires a linear regulator, so I compared three linear options. The pump current does not pass through this regulator.

Option Estimated Unit Cost Pros Cons ST L7805CVDatasheet $1.08 Fixed 5V output keeps the circuit simple.Already included in the schematic.Includes current limiting and thermal protection. Dissipates heat while reducing the supply voltage.May need a heat sink depending on load and mounting.Requires appropriate capacitors and a thermal check. TI LM2940CT-5.0/NOPBDatasheet $2.00 Fixed 5V output.Lower dropout can help when the input is closer to 5V.Through-hole package is convenient for assembly. Higher estimated price.Output capacitance and ESR must meet its requirements.Lower dropout does not remove the heat produced at the same input voltage and load. ST LM317TDatasheet $1.13 Adjustable output.Through-hole package is convenient for assembly.Includes current limiting and thermal protection. Needs resistors to set the output voltage.Resistor tolerance affects the output setting.Adds parts when the design only needs a fixed 5V rail.

Current selection: L7805CV.

Why I chose it: The L7805 provides the fixed 5V output the control circuit needs without an adjustable resistor network. It also meets the assignment’s linear-regulator requirement.

Supporting components: The input and output capacitors support regulator operation and reduce supply disturbances. Local decoupling near the controller helps supply brief changes in current demand. Capacitor values, voltage ratings, and placement need to follow the final regulator and board requirements.

Power and heat: The preliminary budget assumes a 106mA control load and a 10mA allowance for the regulator’s own operating current. Under those assumptions, estimated regulator heat is 0.514W at a 9V input or 0.862W at a 12V input. These are calculated estimates, not measurements or verified maximum values. Actual load, mounting, and temperature will determine whether a heat sink is needed.

The Curiosity Nano external-power configuration must also be verified before connecting the regulator to VTG.

Custom option considered: The regulator and supporting capacitors will be placed on the pump board. A resistor divider cannot maintain a regulated supply as the load changes. A switching regulator could reduce heat, but it would not meet the stated linear-regulator requirement.

docs.title: Flyback Diode — Current MOSFET Circuit
docs.text:
The motor is an inductive load. When the MOSFET turns off, motor current needs a path to continue flowing briefly. The flyback diode provides that path and limits the resulting voltage spike.

Option Estimated Unit Cost Pros Cons Diotec 1N5822Datasheet $0.71 Schottky diode option for motor switching.Listed 3A average-current rating.Listed 40V reverse-voltage rating. Current capability depends on mounting and temperature.Actual motor current must be checked.Protection arrangement must be reconsidered for the H-bridge. Diotec 1N5819Datasheet $0.29 Lowest estimated price.Schottky diode option.Smaller package. Listed 1A average-current rating leaves less current margin.Motor-current pulses may exceed its suitability.Thermal performance still needs checking. Vishay SB560-E3/54Datasheet $1.26 Listed 5A average-current rating.Listed 60V reverse-voltage rating.Through-hole package is convenient for assembly. Highest estimated price.Larger package uses more board space.Additional capacity may be unnecessary after motor current is established.

Component in the current schematic: 1N5822.

Why I chose it: The 1N5822 offers more rated current capacity than the 1N5819 at a lower estimated cost than the SB560. Its suitability still depends on motor current, switching conditions, and temperature.

In the current single-direction circuit, the cathode connects to motor-supply positive. The anode connects to pump negative and the MOSFET drain.

Required revision: This single diode across the motor must not be carried unchanged into a bidirectional H-bridge circuit. It would conduct when motor polarity is reversed. The final H-bridge needs the recirculation paths specified for that driver arrangement.

Custom option considered: Other clamping arrangements could affect how quickly motor current decays. The protection choice must be made with the final motor driver and tested for stopping behavior.

docs.text:
The original design used a 12V adapter to supply the motor and the input of the 5V regulator. These comparisons document that original decision.

The project specifies a 9V adapter. None of the 12V models below is a finalized supply selection for that requirement.

Does not match the specified 9V adapter.Startup current and total load still need checking.Plug compatibility and AC cord requirements need confirmation. MEAN WELL GST40A12-P1JDatasheet $22.93 Listed 12V, 3.34A output.More current capacity than the 25W option.Originally considered if the load exceeded the smaller supply. Does not match the specified 9V adapter.Higher estimated cost.Connectors and wiring still need suitable current ratings. Does not match the specified 9V adapter.Highest estimated cost.Extra supply capacity does not reduce regulator heating.

Original candidate: GST25A12-P1J. Final supply selection: pending.

Why I originally chose it: It provided the planned 12V output at a lower estimated cost than the larger options. That choice was based on the original voltage assumption.

What changes now: The final supply must match the project’s voltage requirement and support the completed load calculation, including motor startup. Barrel-jack size, polarity, fuse, wiring, and connector ratings must match the selected supply.

The preliminary budget gives 616mA operating current, or 770mA with a 25% margin, using explicitly assumed loads. This does not establish the current needed during startup or a stall. It also does not include the final H-bridge demand.

Each board uses a local power connection. The pump board does not receive power through its ribbon connector.

Custom option considered: A commercial enclosed adapter provides the low-voltage input. The local regulation and motor-control circuitry go on our board.

docs.title: Controller and Communication
docs.text:
The current design uses the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, which I already have from lab work. It provides the GPIO needed for the command inputs, motor output, and local debugging. The project allows the Curiosity Nano to be used as the controller.

The main controller sends C1 and C0 as two digital signals. C1 connects from ribbon pin 1 to RC3, and C0 connects from ribbon pin 2 to RC2. Read as C1 C0, 00 = Stop, 01 = Run, 10 = Stop, and 11 = Stop. UART and I²C are not used for inter-board commands.

The main controller receives the system’s measurement information and decides when to stop dispensing. My board controls the motor in response to its commands.

UART and I²C are not used for inter-board commands.

docs.text:

Fuse Intended to limit damage from excessive current; its rating must be checked against startup current and wiring limits. Enable jumper Provides a removable connection in the current motor-control path. Debug LED and series resistor Provides a local visual indicator while limiting LED current. Debug button, pull-up resistor, and capacitor Provides a local test input, a defined released state, and input filtering. Firmware may still need debounce handling. Spare header Makes RD2, RD3, power, and ground available for local testing or a later assigned function. The flyback diode protects against motor-switching transients. It does not provide reverse-polarity protection at the barrel jack.

docs.title: MCC Configuration
docs.text:
I configured the PIC18F57Q43 in MCC Melody and generated the initialization files. These settings match the GPIO connections in my current schematic.

Pin Generated Name Configuration Purpose RC3 PUMP_CMD0 Digital input Command bit from ribbon pin 1. RC2 PUMP_CMD1 Digital input Command bit from ribbon pin 2. RA2 MOTOR_CNTRL Digital output, initially low Controls the current MOSFET circuit. RD0 DEBUG_LED Digital output, initially low External debug LED. RD1 DEBUG_BTN Digital input Debug button with the external pull-up shown in the schematic.

Analog functions, internal weak pull-ups, open-drain outputs, and interrupt-on-change are disabled for these five pins. The internal oscillator is configured for 64MHz. UART, I²C, and PWM are not configured.

Download the MPLAB X project and MCC configuration

Code generation completed successfully. The generated program initializes the system but does not yet interpret commands or operate the pump. Compilation and hardware operation have not been verified. The configuration will need updating when the H-bridge is added.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: My Fill-A-Bot pump subsystem uses a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano to control an R385 pump through a MOSFET switching circuit. It receives a two-bit digital command from the main controller through PUMP_CMD0 on RC3 and PUMP_CMD1 on RC2. The board includes a local power input, 5 V regulator, fuse, flyback diode, and debugging components. The current motor circuit supports one-direction operation; forward/reverse control remains a planned revision.

docs.title: Power Supply
docs.text:
Power enters through barrel jack J1 and fuse F1. U1 is the L7805 regulator that provides the planned 5 V supply for the controller. C1 and C2 help keep the regulator input and output stable. C4 provides additional decoupling near the controller.

My current schematic uses a 12 V input. I still need to resolve that choice with the course requirement for a 9 V adapter.

docs.title: Command Inputs
docs.text:
The main board sends commands to my pump board using two digital signals. Each signal can be HIGH or LOW, giving four possible combinations. The finalized pump command is read as C1 C0: 00 = Stop, 01 = Run, 10 = Stop, and 11 = Stop. C1 enters through J3 pin 1 at RC3, and C0 enters through J3 pin 2 at RC2. The pump runs only while the command is 01.

Signal Connector PIC port PUMP_CMD0 J3 pin 1 RC3 PUMP_CMD1 J3 pin 2 RC2 Shared ground J3 pin 8 GND

RC2 and RC3 will be set as digital inputs in firmware. The UART text on the PIC symbol lists another function those pins can perform.

The ribbon uses pins 1–5 for digital I/O, pins 6–7 for analog, and pin 8 for ground. Each board has its own power connection.

docs.title: Pump Control
docs.text:
The PIC controls Q1 through its RA2 output, jumper JP1, and resistor R1. Q1 acts as a switch in the pump's return path to ground. This lets the PIC control the pump without carrying the motor current through a GPIO pin.

R1 limits current into the MOSFET gate during switching. R2 pulls the gate toward ground when it is not driven, helping keep Q1 off. D1 gives the motor current a path when Q1 switches off. The pump connects at J2.

Opening JP1 disconnects the PIC from the gate-drive path so that connection can be isolated during testing.

docs.title: Testing and Spare Connections
docs.text:
D2 is a debug LED with current-limiting resistor R3. SW1 provides a local button input, with R4 pulling the input high and C3 providing filtering. I still need to define the LED and button functions in the program.

J4 brings out spare GPIO pins, 5 V, and ground for local testing or expansion.

docs.title: Changes Still Needed
docs.text: The current MOSFET circuit controls the pump in one direction. I still need to revise the driver for forward and reverse operation and check whether the selected pump can move water in reverse. The supply voltage and command meanings also need to be finalized.

docs.title: Preliminary Design Estimate
docs.text:
This budget uses the course spreadsheet template for my pump board. I have the Curiosity Nano and basic lab components, but I do not have the pump yet. The current values are planning assumptions, not measurements or verified maximum ratings.

The calculation uses a 9V input to match the project requirement. My current schematic still shows 12V and needs to be updated after the supply and pump choices are resolved.

Load Assumed current Basis Proposed R385 pump 500mA Placeholder for operating-load planning; startup and stall current unknown. Complete Curiosity Nano 100mA Whole-board planning allowance, not a datasheet maximum or measured value. External debug LED 5mA Upper-bound allowance using the 5V rail and 1kΩ series resistor. Other control loads 1mA Allowance for pull-ups and gate drive; switching configuration still needs verification. L7805 own operating current 10mA Planning allowance, not a verified maximum.

docs.title: Results Under These Assumptions
docs.text:
Result Calculated value 5V control load 106mA 5V load with 25% margin 132.5mA Regulator input current, including own operating current 116mA Total adapter operating current 616mA Adapter current with 25% margin 770mA Adapter operating input power at 9V 5.544W Regulator heat at 9V, including assumed own current 0.514W Regulator heat at original 12V assumption 0.862W

The pump receives motor-supply power directly. Its current does not pass through the 5V regulator. The source total includes the regulator input current once; it does not add the 5V load again.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
These assumptions give a preliminary source requirement of 770mA after a 25% margin. That number does not establish that an adapter will start the motor or handle a stall. The adapter model and current rating remain unselected.

The budget must be revised using the actual pump current and the final H-bridge design. H-bridge losses and control demand are not included yet. Regulator temperature and the Nano external-power configuration also need verification. The regulator heat estimates do not establish that a heat sink is unnecessary.

No battery or separate 3.3V rail is used. Other team boards are outside this individual budget, and the ribbon connector does not supply their power.
